speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall have to oppose this motion and I wish to say with reference to it that I have already indicated to the house that I communicated certain information respecting the estate of the late John T. Drohan to the premier of Ontario in his capacity as provincial treasurer, under the agreement between the governments of Ontario and Canada, which has already been tabled in the house. That agreement provided for the exchange of information concerning provincial and federal succession duties.
By the terms of the Dominion Succession Duty Act I am under an obligation not to disclose any such information to anyone whomsoever who is not entitled by law to receive it. In this, as in all other matters, I have scrupulously refrained from disclosing such information to anybody not entitled by law to receive it. I therefore cannot be held responsible for recent publicity which has occurred in relation to what is alleged to be information lawfully disclosed by me.
In view of the express provisions of the Dominion Succession Duty Act I am unable to comply with the request now made of me that I disclose any such information to the house or any committee of the house. Because of the statutory bar the government has no option but to oppose this motion and also the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

Inquiries of the Ministry whether any progress was made at the conference held in Halifax on May 20 in regard to keeping 1-B colliery at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, operating after May 30; and second, was any progress made in regard to securing additional markets for the Nova Scotia coal industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESULT OF RECENT MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Cape Breton South for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question.
At the invitation of the government of Nova Scotia a meeting was held in Halifax on Friday, May 20, with the premier of Nova Scotia in the chair, to review the problem presented by the closure of No. 1-B colliery at Glace Bay. My hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Ivlac-Eachen), and I attended this meeting, accompanied by officials of the Department of Labour and the dominion coal board. Also present were representatives of the provincial government, the executive of district 26, united mine workers, and executive officers of the Dominion Coal Company.
The problems of finding markets for the coal from this and other collieries of the area were most carefully studied. The effect on the market for coal of imports of low cost residual fuel oil was reviewed, and the possibility of developing additional outlets for coal was thoroughly canvassed. The effects on the life and economy of the area of the projected closure were brought out, and the problems of finding alternative employment for over 700 miners affected were stressed.
The meeting was investigatory only, and I can report that factors that could have a bearing on this difficult situation were brought forward and carefully examined. One promising line of investigation having to do with markets abroad was developed and is being intensively pursued at the present time by the Dominion Coal Company, the dominion coal board and officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
If successful this may enable the company to maintain this colliery in operation without causing additional difficulties in the marketing of coal from other collieries in the province. I expect to be able to report upon this at a later date, possibly when the estimates of the dominion coal board are before the committee; but since the negotiations are presently under way I would prefer to avoid being more specific at the present time.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 24, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Lesage-Mr. Robinson (Sim-coe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to repeal the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, chapter 301 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, and to make provision by means of a new act for all substantive rights relating to quartz mining in the Yukon, including the rights to stake and acquire mineral claims and leases, and to provide for certain modifications in the administration of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL EXISTING LEGISLATION AND SUBSTITUTE NEW ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the adjournment last night I was about to outline the recommendations of Mr. Cole, which formed the basis of the legislation which this resolution seeks to introduce. The first recommendation is that there should be no change in the placer mining act at this time. I have already mentioned this last night.
The second recommendation deals with the question of whether quartz mining in the Yukon should be governed by statute or regulation. Mr. Cole recommended against the original plan to cover mining in the Yukon entirely by regulation. He stated that the Yukon mining fraternity wanted to have the essential privileges of prospectors safe-
Yukon Quartz Mining Act guarded by statutory provisions. The recommendation of Mr. Cole was as follows:
I therefore recommend that the rights of the prospector to prospect and stake claims anywhere in the Yukon Territory be protected by statute and that all administrative procedures of such prospecting and staking, including the number and size of claims, the method of staking, the use of cairns, the recording of claims, the granting of leases and all other matters connected with the disposal of mining rights should be provided for by regulations.
The bill has been drafted along those lines. All the substantive provisions of the present act are covered by sections of the bill to be introduced. The administrative procedures will be provided for by regulation of the governor in council. The result will be to give full and adequate protection to all matters of substance. Such matters cannot be changed without an act of parliament.
As a matter of fact we shall have put rather more into the statute than Mr. Cole recommended. For instance, in the act will be a provision as to the number of claims that can be staked, a provision as to the size of claims, and much of the procedure of an important character with regard to the recording of claims will also be in the act. This is to ensure full protection to the Yukon prospectors.
I want to give the assurance that the placing of procedural matters in regulations will not in any way endanger the privileges now enjoyed by prospectors. I wish to stress that only the detailed procedures of administration will be governed by regulation. The compromise recommended by Mr. Cole and embodied in the bill will provide for flexibility in administrative procedures, but will assure protection of substantive rights.
Regulations in respect to the administration of natural resources are not new to the people in the Yukon Territory. The Territorial Lands Act is applicable to the Yukon. Lands, as far as surface rights are concerned, timber, oil and gas rights, quarrying, dredging for minerals, are all administered by regulations. One of the pertinent recommendations of Mr. Cole deals with the question of withdrawing areas from ordinary staking, and to grant reservations or concessions by public competitions. This is an important matter. The virtue of that procedure is that it enables an area that is capable of development only on a large scale and at high cost to be bid on by companies which have the resources to develop it.

speechtext:
I am talking about mineral development-quartz mining. The procedure

Yukon Quartz Mining Act is often of distinct advantage for the development of a region. In answer to the hon. member for Yukon I might say that the Pine Point development is a good example of the necessity at times of granting so-called concessions. The Pine Point concession in the Northwest Territories is really much too large to be developed by small holders, and it is susceptible of development only on a very large scale. The granting of reservations or concessions often encourages capital and enterprise to come into a region. However, there has been and there is considerable opposition in the Yukon to the governor in council having any right to grant concessions or reservations.
Mr. Cole recommended:
I believe that a healthy condition exists in the Yukon in so far as the individual prospector is concerned and that the time has not yet come when "the governor in council should be given the right to withdraw areas in the Yukon Territory from ordinary staking or to grant reservations or concessions by public competition."
I would recommend that the granting of reservations or concessions be reviewed if and when conditions change.
Since, as I have said, in this new bill we are following the recommendations of the Cole report, the bill to be introduced consequently contains no provision to enable concessions or reservations being granted. This is also due to the objections we have received from the prospectors in the Yukon, and to the objections that were very strongly made by the hon. member for Yukon himself.
The fourth recommendation of the Cole report deals with the method of staking. Under the present act claims staked in the Yukon require only two posts to be marked; that is to say, a location line is established. The rest of the claim is supposed to be a square based on that line. All corners of the claim are not marked on the ground. The so-called two-post staking or single-line staking is such that the boundaries of the claim are not marked.
An important question referred to Mr. Cole was whether this should be done away with and four-post staking substituted. Four-post staking requires the marking of all four corners of a claim and the establishment of all four sides. As a matter of fact, only the Yukon, British Columbia and Alberta now have two-post staking. The Northwest Territories and all other provinces have four-post staking. If we go across the border we find that Alaska, Utah, Colorado, Oregon, Nevada and many other states have four-post staking or even more than four-post staking, and require all boundaries to be marked.
There are some prospectors in the Yukon who are much attached to the two-post

staking. I know the hon. member for Yukon disagrees with Mr. Cole on that score and I expect him to give reasons for two-post staking.

Mr. Cole went into that question of four-post and two-post staking very fully, and I believe it is worth putting on record his recommendation and his conclusion on that score:
In the final analysis the strongest argument used in favour of two-post staking is that it is better adapted to the rugged western terrain. In fact, it is about the only reasonable argument offered. That it is easy, simple and quick is hardly acceptable where a matter of acquiring title to mineral

land is involved. And with changing conditions in the acquisition of mineral claims, the fact that the two-post method has been used for years does not measure up to modern needs. Nor is the four-post staking any more difficult to understand than the two-post method, although it must be admitted that it demands more work. All of which prompts the inclusion of a question asked by a prospector, "Do you want to do it right or do you want to do it easy?"
I am still quoting Mr. Cole's report:
I am of the opinion that four-post staking can be and should be used in the Yukon Territory despite the many areas of rugged terrain.
I am convinced further that if the prospecting fraternity of the Yukon accept the four-post staking as an endeavour to improve the prospector-purchaser relations in their territory, it should stimulate the interest of those financially able to develop the mineral resources of the Yukon, to the mutual advantage of all concerned.
The present Yukon Quartz Mining Act, section 26, has provisions for the staking out of a claim "in case it is found impossible, owing to the presence of water or other insurmountable obstacle to set post No. 2 in its proper position ..." etc.
I am confident if study be made of this provision for witness posts then an effective plan can be devised for four-post staking.
However, some suggestion has been made that the two-post staking could be used in some areas and the four-post in others. This would not be a compromise, rather would it lead to more confusion.
In my opinion it is one method or the other, and I have expressed myself as being in favour of four-post staking.
The bill does not include a clause dealing with the method of staking. It will not be in the bill. This is, as the Cole report recommends, a procedural matter. However, as it is a question of importance I wish to make clear now what the Cole report says and what is the intention as to what will be the regulations and what will be in the new act.
The fifth recommendation of the Cole report had to do with the surveying of claims. I quote the recommendation:
I am of the opinion that the minister should have the right to demand that an unsurveyed claim be surveyed within a reasonable time-depending on the circumstances that may arise.
The new act will provide for this. The old act also provided for the same thing.
The sixth recommendation deals with the requirement to take out leases. The present act does not require leases to be taken out after any specified period or even before substantial mining operations occur. We do not believe it is satisfactory to have claims remaining simply as claims indefinitely. In his report Mr. Cole recommended:
A limit of ten years after the recording of a claim be set as that at which a claim holder should take out a lease.
And in order that those presently holding claims may be brought to comply with a time limit, such as may be applied to future claim holders, I would suggest further that present claim holders
Yukon Quartz Mining Act be given a period of ten years-from, say July 1, 1954 (or such other date as may be found advisable), to take out leases so that all claim holders may be on the same basis.
The bill will provide accordingly.
I have now given a brief summary of the recommendations of the Cole report. I have gone into them in detail because they form the basis of the proposed legislation. I wish to emphasize, however, that they are not simply the views of one man. Last night I cited the great experience of Mr. Cole, one of the best qualified men in Canada to give an expert opinion on these questions.

2.	Areas of the Yukon Territory should not be withdrawn from ordinary staking to grant reservations or concessions.
We agree with him entirely on this point.
3.	A system of four-post staking similar to that now in effect in eastern Canada and Alaska should replace the existing two-post, single line method now in effect in the Yukon and British Columbia.
4.	A time limit should be set within which a claim owner must have his mineral claim surveyed.

They sent Colonel Cole to the Yukon last summer to make an inquiry. What did he do? Well, he reported to the minister to the effect that the mining industry were quite happy with the Yukon Placer Mining Act, "so leave it alone." You must realize that there is one company up there trying to get the mining laws changed and that is the reason.
It is agreed that some minor amendments are required to the existing act. However, there appears to be no necessity to scrap an excellent act that is most popular among the large number of prospectors and other mining people. It is felt that the wishes and opinions of the large majority of practical mining people active in the Yukon should be considered and that the proposed legislation along the lines of Colonel Cole's recommendations should be reconsidered.
It is the considered and practically unanimous opinion that the granting of reservations or concessions of mineral lands in the Yukon Territory, the arbitrary enactment of four-post staking and repeal of the present two-post staking, the endorsement of compulsory surveys of mineral claims and compulsory applications for leases would be contrary to the true spirit of free enterprise, resulting in unjustifiable hardships to the prospecting and mining fraternity domiciled in the Yukon and in several years of confusion, uncertainty and frustration. Therefore, in my opinion, any proposed legislative action should be confined to amendments to the existing act.

I find it difficult to reconcile certain aspects of Colonel Cole's investigation. For example, why was he selected for this task and who made the selection? Without reflecting in any way on his proven integrity and ability, it is a fact nevertheless that he has indicated in his tenure of office with the Manitoba department of mines that he long has been a proponent of four-post staking and regulations rather than the stability of an act.
Further, why select an individual from one of the only three areas of Canada where mining is administered under regulations rather than someone from the several provinces where at least 90 per cent of metal mining is done and where mining administration under an act has been well proven. Better still, why not an individual from the area involved in such investigation?
Two-post staking is a time-tested, proven and entirely adequate method of establishing claims in such mountainous areas as British Columbia and the Yukon. I am surprised that Alaska should be cited by Colonel Cole as an illustration of the practicability of four-post or seven-post staking.
We are all aware that this is simply a direct and natural extension of the practice within the United States and, unfortunately, is practically impossible to change now. It might well be noted in this connection that these laws were inherited in part originally from the Spanish and are widely admitted by United States authorities to be most unsatisfactory and, in fact, almost unworkable.
Surely under these circumstances we can well afford to look to Alaskan practice as evidence in support of two-post staking. It might also be noted that there is currently a very strong sentiment among the mining fraternity of Alaska for a change in the method of staking.
In spite of the kindly sentiment expressed in regard to the prospector there seems little hesitation in burdening him with considerable unnecessary work and expense in four-post staking. In this matter also Colonel Cole's opinion disregards the will of the majority entirely.
If some of these four-post proponents would refer to Dent's Canadian School Atlas of 1940 they would see some very fine reference maps of the Canadian provinces which were compiled by the Edinburgh Geographical Institute. These relief maps show that the greater part of Manitoba and all of Ontario and the greater part of Quebec have elevations of 2,000 feet or less.
Compare these elevations with the topography of western Alberta, British Columbia

and Yukon Territory. I might point out, Mr. Chairman, that Kluane lake in the Yukon has an elevation of 2,525 feet above sea level while mount Logan not far to the southwest of lake Kluane has an elevation of 19,850 feet. Or step clear across the Yukon to Frances lake, the elevation of which is 2,000 feet, and from the head of the east arm of this lake one may walk to the summit which has an elevation of around 9,000 feet.
How would some of these four-post proponents like to put four posts on the top of it? It would, no doubt, teach them to be more sympathetic and considerate of their fellow man.
Whatever the geographical and topographical aspects may be in eastern Canada it is certain that in the Yukon and in British Columbia these conditions are such as to make four-post staking a practical impossibility.
If anyone has ever staked claims in mountainous country they will be forced to admit it would be virtually impossible to stake out four corners of a claim with any degree of accuracy. Even in a flat country like Ontario claims are by no means square, or even of any particular shape.
All one has to do to verify this statement is to look over a claim map of some of the older districts, say Kirkland Lake for instance. It is at least 1,000 times more difficult to set out a square in the mountainous areas of British Columbia or the Yukon. With two-post staking and a reasonably accurate map as a guide one can pretty well tell the location of any claim.
The four or seven-post staking required in Alaska was cited. The complaints one hears about this method in Alaska and in the western states, where similar requirements are in force, would certainly lead one to the conclusion that stakers would much prefer the two-post method of British Columbia or the Yukon.
Some of Colonel Cole's objections to two-post staking are really amusing. It is infinitely simpler to run a survey along one boundary if overstaking has occurred than to have to run four boundaries of each claim to determine just how much overlap has occurred. Further, if his fear of fractions is as great as indicated, then all that is required is to stake out one of each four claims as a fractional claim to begin with, and claim all open ground up to 60 acres.
Colonel Cole does not differentiate between legitimate staking and wildcat staking. During a boom anyone who purchases claims for more than a nominal sum without first of all having a survey of some kind run 50433-259
Yukon Quartz Mining Act deserves to lose his money. Sorting out holdings staked out under the two-stake per claim method is easier, cheaper and quicker than with four posts as he suggests. Even under boom conditions, a prospector always knows the discovery he has made is covered by his claims when staking by the two-post method. In almost every case he will stake along the strike, throwing a claim each side of his location line. If he follows along the outcrops he will not let any showings escape him. He would be a poor staker if he wandered over 1,500 feet from the strike of the deposit or deposits he is staking in that same distance.
As a rule the original discoverer of any mine receives little or nothing for his labours, probably having had to sell out long before he should have done owing to economic stresses. Then-and this has never yet been made clear-who are those interested who desire revision of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, and who wish to force upon us four-post staking, regulations, compulsory surveys and compulsory applications for leases? Naturally, I am puzzled about the mysterious "easterners". There seems to be an implication that the two-post system is causing "easterners" to withhold from participation in new found exploration and mining. What a joke!

Further, surveys are expensive, and the average prospector does not have funds available for that kind of work, but is well able to handle his assessment work as it consists largely of his own labour. To have a claim surveyed in the Yukon would cost about $500 per claim, the equivalent of five years' assessment work, and the claim owner only gets credit for one year's work. If they are going to reduce the size of our claims, it is going to cost a prospector much more. I cannot understand it at all.
Such a requirement would be confiscatory as far as the average prospector goes. If the claims are of sufficient value, then the purchasers from the prospector will see they are surveyed to protect themselves. Very few discretionary powers are left to the whims and fancies of government officials, and even those powers are sometimes abused. They are still waiting. In most cases all that is ever done with a concession is to give it "a lick and a promise". If the first results are not satisfactory the officials of large companies lose heart, and are generally afraid to ask for further funds, the net result being large areas are damned outright or with faint praise, and are eliminated from the possible areas others will look over. Concessions would hog the mineral potentialities of the country to the detriment of individual prospectors and syndicates. Concessions always tend to hold back rather than to encourage prospecting and the discovery of new deposits.
For many years past mining in the Yukon Territory has been administered under the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and the Yukon Placer Mining Act. The people of the Yukon

have been very happy with these acts which have been kept up to date with modern developments by occasional amending acts of parliament. This has meant that all proposed changes in mining legislation have been brought out into the open and have been thoroughly discussed by members of this house. The people of the Yukon want their mining laws administered under acts wherein any proposed changes would be presented to and discussed in parliament. There is general agreement that some further minor amendments should be made in the present act in order to deal with problems which have come to light in recent years. But the people are unanimous in their desire to have our mining laws governed by an act and not by regulations in any degree.
Let us go back into some history of how this happy state of affairs occurred, because things were not always so happy in the Yukon prior to 1924 when our mining laws were administered by regulations under orders in council. Back in 1898 mining matters in the Yukon were administered by regulations passed by orders in council. This procedure caused so much dissatisfaction with and resentment of the administration of mining that in 1900 Mr. Justice Britton of the supreme court of Ontario was sent to the Yukon to study placer mining problems. As a result of the consideration given to the problems at that time the Yukon Placer Mining Act was enacted in 1906. This act has given entire satisfaction. There are no regulations under this act.
Perhaps I should explain that at that time placer mining was the dominant industry and held the centre of interest in the Yukon Territory, and that people did not become interested in quartz mining until after 1906 when quartz mining continued to be administered under regulations. I might also mention the fact that there was very little interest in quartz mining at that time in the Northwest Territories, Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta.
Another point of interest is that there was throughout Canada general dissatisfaction with the administration of mining matters by regulations and under orders in council. This dissatisfaction was so widespread that the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy presented a brief to the government in 1910 advocating the administration of mining laws by means of an act of parliament.
As a result the Canada mines act was prepared for the twelfth Canadian parliament upon principles advocated by that institution, and was introduced in this house in 1912. Had that act passed there would have been 50433-259J
Yukon Quartz Mining Act no necessity for the Yukon Quartz Mining Act which was enacted in 1924. Unfortunately the Canada mines act of 1912 was not passed.
The point I wish to make, Mr. Chairman, is that for over 50 years the people of Canada who are interested in developing the mineral resources of this country, wherever they may be, have advocated the administration of mining laws under acts of parliament-and have always been opposed to the instability created by administration under regulations -so that today mining matters in all provinces where there is any degree of mining activity, such as Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, administer their mining laws under acts of provincial parliaments.
Let us now go back to the Yukon Territory and see what happened to quartz mining there. As I told you previously there was very little activity in quartz mining in 1906 when the Yukon Placer Mining Act was passed, so there was no great concern whether quartz mining was administered under an act of parliament or under regulations which could be changed overnight without the foreknowledge or approval of the mining industry. However, the quartz mining industry was soon due for a decided change and acceleration in pace. It picked up rapidly and public dissatisfaction with and resentment of administration by regulations and orders in council developed. Public feeling and resentment to this unhappy state of affairs developed to such an extent that in 1924 the mining industry in general became dissatisfied, distrustful and aroused by administration by regulations so that the Liberal government of the day allowed an opposition member, the Hon. George Black, to
sponsor the Yukon Quartz Mining Act__________a
highly popular and time-tested act-which was approved by parliament. There is no provision for the arbitrary enactment of regulations under this act, something for which we are truly thankful. That is the way we want to keep it.
Despite all this history, not only in the Yukon Territory but throughout the provinces, of public disapproval and resentment of the administration of mining matters by regulations, and the almost universal desire to have mining matters stabilized under acts of parliament, the government has apparently decided that it knows much better about what is good for the mining industry in the Yukon than does the industry itself. What did it do? In 1952 the government brought in a bill to repeal both the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and the Yukon Placer Mining Act. This bill was introduced in the other place but it died in the House of Commons. Since then.

Yukon Quartz Mining Act I am sure it has been realized that the proposed repeal of those two acts was a mistake.
The intention was to extend the Northwest Territories mining regulations to the Yukon Territory. This bill was introduced without my knowledge and without consulting anyone in the Yukon Territory. In other words, the people of the Yukon were going to take this dose of medicine whether they liked it or not. Fortunately this bill died in the house. I say "fortunately" because I cannot conceive how any action could have been more highhanded, unpopular and undemocratic.
Let me again emphasize the fact that in 1952 the government intended to repeal both the Yukon Placer Mining Act and the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. Now it intends to leave the Yukon Placer Mining Act alone, while it still obstinately continues to insist on forcing upon us distasteful legislation by completely revising our Yukon quartz mining laws, because that is what this proposed legislation intends to do. Why it is being done is beyond my comprehension and, as you must have gathered, it is against my advice and the wishes of the overwhelming majority of the people of the Yukon.
The Yukon Quartz Mining Act, passed in 1924, has been an admirable act.

It certainly is. It has been, it is yet and it always will be. It was framed with the assistance and the advice of the mining fraternity-both the prospectors and mining companies-and it has met the situation peculiar to the Yukon. We must remember that the Yukon is different topographically from any other section of Canada except the province of British Columbia. It was therefore natural that the Yukon Quartz Mining Act should follow the pattern which had been developed for British Columbia, and with which the prospectors were thoroughly familiar.
In the Yukon Territory mining is an old industry and the prospectors and miners and people working in it have developed over the years, by trial and error and the sweat of their brows, and experience in the conditions peculiar to the territory, a set of mining laws which they know and understand, and with which they are generally satisfied. I am sure that all hon. members can plainly see why they are reluctant to have our mining laws tampered with.
In any legislation which we pass with a view to assisting mining resources development, we must be sure that annoying details of legislation are eliminated. In these days

when there is so much criticism of legislation by regulations it is easy to understand why the Yukon people, who have been quite satisfied with the Yukon quartz and placer mining acts, are reluctant to see any drastic amendments such as have been proposed to our mining laws on the recommendation of Colonel Cole. May I have leave of the house, Mr. Chairman, to continue for another three or four minutes?

speechtext:
The mining fraternity does not want the lauded flexibility of regulations which can be changed overnight without their knowledge, and often to their detriment, in place of the stability of an act. I share their view that there is everything to be said in favour of retaining the present mining acts rather than administering our mining laws in part by regulations. Undoubtedly the retention of the present act, with slight amendments to bring it up to date, would be preferable and in the interests of mining resources development in the Yukon. The adoption of regulations in part, in lieu of the stability of an act, is certainly a retrograde step in our democratic form of government.
It is quite obvious, therefore, that as soon as we have sufficient population and industry the people in the territories will welcome self-government which will enable them to run their own affairs as they deem fit, and consistent with the wishes and needs of the people of the particular areas, rather than have forced upon them distasteful legislation which they do not wish to accept. Surely the government is not going to completely ignore the wishes of the people in this regard.
Amendments to the Yukon Quartz Mining Act at the present time have to be submitted to parliament and so become known to the electors and to the people affected by them. If these laws are revised and regulations substituted in part for them, parliament cannot be consulted or informed as to what the government is doing and has no opportunity to approve, object or offer amendments. In other words, it will rob parliament of its power, and this will be most unpopular in the Yukon. Any part of the proposed new act providing for regulations will be most

unsatisfactory as it is generally felt that the present act has been working satisfactorily for a number of years and that any changes necessary should be confined to the existing act rather than be made by a revision with enactment by regulations.
The Yukon Quartz Mining Act, as I have said before, is a very good one. With a few minor changes it is as good as, if not better than, any mining act in Canada, and the mining can be carried on very satisfactorily under it. Again let me reiterate that I am unequivocally opposed to regulations in any form in so far as they relate to our mining laws, as I believe in the business of the country being carried on under statutes as much as possible. We have heard very few complaints from prospectors or mine operators regarding our mining laws.
At the present time prospectors and mining development are more active in the Yukon than ever before, with quite a number of additional companies planning to operate in that area during the coming season. More and more prospectors are also looking to the Yukon as a favourable area in which to search for mineral deposits. The mining fraternity is entirely familiar with the Yukon Quartz Mining Act on the whole and are satisfied with its provisions and the protection it affords them. So why change it? To my way of thinking the present act is a pretty fair mining act, far better than it would be if altered to suit Mr. Cole's way of thinking, which leads me to believe that the less some government officials have to do with administering our mining laws by regulations the better and more smoothly business can be carried on.
There are a few government officials who do not have any grasp of the true conditions of business, and certainly not of prospecting or mining. They fall into two types, those who become very arbitrary and insist on deciding everything according to their personal views, or those who are afraid to make any decisions. The present act is pretty definite on almost all subjects and should, therefore, not be altered to give officials more discretionary powers, for that can only lead to abuse. The administration of the mining laws in the Yukon prior to 1924 will bear me out in these views.
I cannot conscientiously support this resolution, Mr. Chairman, against the wishes of the people of the Yukon who are bitterly opposed to the recommendations contained in the Cole report as a basis for any proposed drastic changes in our mining laws. The prospecting and mining industry must be safeguarded and unhampered by mandatory
Yukon Quartz Mining Act orders emanating several thousand miles distant from the scene of mining operations m the territory. I have refrained from extreme statements as I do not wish anything I have said to be interpreted as meaning that I am personally hostile to the minister presenting the resolution.

On an earlier occasion the minister defended himself by taking the position that he would not interfere with what was done by a regulation of the territorial council. Today, on this other measure, he is taking the position that he will not listen to the Yukon territorial council; he is ignoring the stand that they have taken on this question. If there is to be democracy in the Yukon, as there is in the rest of Canada, then I suggest that the hon. member for the Yukon and the members of the territorial council are the ones whose advice should have been taken on this question and not the recommendation of an engineer from Manitoba.
The hon. member for the Yukon has read extracts from letters from the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines. Some hon. members might wonder why it is that there is

a chamber of mines that deals with mining both in British Columbia and in the Yukon. The reason is that there is the closest association between miners in British Columbia and in the Yukon Territory. The territory was opened largely by prospectors and miners from British Columbia. The hon. member for Yukon, himself, is a native son of British Columbia. Until the construction of the Alaska highway all the traffic to the Yukon went up the west coast from Vancouver, Victoria, and the other coastal ports and eventually got by rail from Skagway into the Yukon. The Alaska highway, too, starts in British Columbia and runs across the northeastern portion of our province into the Yukon Territory. Air connection to the Yukon is also made from Vancouver, although there is in addition an air service from Edmonton into the territory.
In mining matters British Columbia and the Yukon have been closely associated for the last half century, and that is why they have this chamber of mines dealing with problems facing the miners in the two areas. As the hon. member has said, the topography of the Yukon and of British Columbia is much the same. The highest mountains in Canada, I believe, are in the Yukon Territory. They are far higher than those in British Columbia.
Many years ago, about the turn of the century, the British Columbia legislature placed on the statute books a mineral act which was a codification of mining laws, and it has been eminently satisfactory ever since. Before that mineral act became law there was litigation of all kinds over mining claims. In fact, most of the litigation in the province had to do with mining. But once that act was placed on the statute books, mining litigation fell away, with the result that since that time the lawyers have had a hard time making any money out of mining disputes in my province.
There have been no regulations under that act; everything is written into the act. It refers to the method of staking and the other details in connection with staking-everything is written into the act. And as the hon. member for Yukon has said, Yukon adopted the same system some years ago. You see, one of the big difficulties about having regulations rather than having everything written into a statute is that those regulations may be interpreted one way today and another way tomorrow. Furthermore they may be changed. The cabinet may meet and decide to make a change, and this can be done. There is not the same difficulty in the matter of permanence and stability when the law is
Yukon Quartz Mining Act placed on the statute books, rather than having it in the form of regulations.
I do not think there is any doubt that the people of the Yukon feel as the hon. member has stated about the possibility of having part of the mineral law made up of regulations. When the bill introduced late in 1953 was under consideration a wire was received from the Hon. George Black who, as hon. members know, for many years represented the Yukon here in the House of Commons, as did also his charming wife, Martha Black. She was here from 1935 to 1940.
The Hon. Mr. Black had this to say about substituting orders in council for statute mining law in the Yukon:
That will be most unsatisfactory to Yukon miners. It is reverting to dictatorship of early days.
Many members in the chamber this afternoon knew George Black, and most people in Canada know his record. I suggest his views on the subject should carry great weight, just as should the views of the hon. member who now represents the Yukon.

I do not think much weight has been attached to Mr. Black's proposals because Mr. Cole has been able to ride roughshod over all such recommendations.
And that brings me to Mr. Cole's report, where he says that he is in favour of four-post staking. I might point out that in British Columbia we have had two-post staking since the enactment of our mineral act. Under that system a prospector can stake out eight claims by placing posts in five different spots. For example, for one claim he will put a stake at one side or one corner, and the next stake 1,500 feet away; then he can claim 1,500 feet out from those stakes. By putting two other stakes beside those two he can claim 1,500 feet in the opposite direction. The result is that he can stake eight claims with 16 stakes; but in order to do that he has to be in only five different spots on the mountainside.
On the other hand, under the four-stake system he would have to put a stake at every corner. Today the minister has mentioned groups of 12 claims. Under the two-stake system the prospector would have to drive in only 24 stakes, many of them driven beside each other, whereas if the four-stake system were used he would have to set out

Yukon Quartz Mining Act 48 stakes. So I say this is an extremely serious matter for prospectors, and it is extremely unfair that men in the Yukon should be forced to work under a system of that kind. .
The reasons given by Mr. Cole for his recommendations are very enlightening, because I believe they go to the root of this whole matter. I turn to that portion of his report which bears the heading, "Two and four-post staking, which?" He says:
This question proved to be the most contentious given to me for investigation. There is a marked division of opinion between the westerners and easterners as to the merits of the two methods . . .
Those prospectors who had lived in British Columbia or the Yukon have grown up with two-post staking. Yet it is passing strange-
And I suggest the use of those very words in this man's report shows how biased he is ail the way through. And he uses words of this kind at more than one place in his report-sarcastic, sneering words about any suggestion in favour of two-post staking. He says:
Yet it is passing strange that in a terrain as rugged as either British Columbia or the Yukon, Alaska has held to the four-post method-or should it be referred to as "seven-post" for three more posts are required to designate the location line.
The hon. member for the Yukon has explained that the Alaska miners wish they did not have this seven-post staking system. Then Mr. Cole goes on to say:
The westerner views his two-post method with a fervour almost vehement-
And again we see a sneering remark about these western prospectors.
-and one at least has voiced his disregard to an eastern counterpart in the words, "If you don't like two-post staking out here you had better go back east."
What kind of statement was this for a responsible man to put in a report to the government? Then it goes on to say:
However an easterner describes it this way, "If a prospector is selling claims that he hasn't got-"
And there again, another sneering remark, insinuating that these prospectors are trying to sell claims they do not own.
"-the two-post staking is wonderful."
And then he goes on to say:
Now the eastern exploration and development companies have moved into the Yukon in search of minerals. They are used to the four-line staking which prevails in all parts of Canada east of Alberta.
The hon. member for Yukon has given evidence today that practically all of these companies actually working in the Yukon are satisfied with the two-post staking system. Mr. Cole goes on to say:
The easterner with the wherewithal-


And here come the money interests, the Toronto stock exchange, and so on-
-to carry on exploration and development is sensitive of the fact that the four-post staking has merits that the westerner fails to appreciate.
And then there is this remarkable paragraph, again showing his bias:
Attention has already been directed to the fact that the money for exploration and development is coming from outside and particularly from the east. What are the points of contention that eastern interests desire to have settled? They feel that the four-post staking offers a measure of security of tenure that is lacking in the two-post staking. It is reasonable-
And here he is speaking for the eastern interests.
-then, for the interests putting up the money to ask the people of the Yukon to co-operate in this regard.
The minister has accepted this report. In other words, the miners in the Yukon are to be sacrificed for the benefit of eastern interests. It is just that simple. That is the statement by this Mr. Cole in his report to the government which report the minister has seen fit to accept.
I suggest that that is a most flimsy foundation upon which to work out a new quartz mining law for the Yukon. The minister will never get the approval or support of the mining people in the Yukon for a measure based on recommendations of that kind. That one recommendation itself should have been enough to condemn Mr. Cole's report. The minister should have called in his own member and the members of the Yukon territorial council and taken advice from them instead of trying to ram this measure down the throats of the people of the Yukon.
I suggest that after the bill has been introduced the fair thing to do would be to allow it to stand until next year. Let us see exactly what the minister has in mind; let these people in the Yukon have the necessary time to study the bill and of course let the eastern interests study it as well. That cannot be done between now and the end of the session. The minister talks about having the bill referred to a committee but that would mean that the bill would be law within the next week or two if the government members stood by the government as they have a fixed habit of doing. It certainly would not give the people of the Yukon an opportunity to check the merits and demerits of this bill. I suggest that nobody would be hurt particularly if that course were followed. Let the bill be introduced and then let it lie on the table so that it may be considered by everybody interested. Then next year amendments

could be put through the house which will give satisfaction to the great majority of the people.
Certainly any measure that passes this house should above all give satisfaction to the people of the Yukon. They are the ones who live in the territory; they are the ones who believe in the territory; and it will be by their efforts that the Yukon will grow and eventually become a province of Canada. But you will never be able to build a province in that northwestern part of Canada by ignoring their wishes, as is being done in this instance, and forcing through legislation against their recommendation.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the committee because I know that at least a dozen members are waiting to speak on this resolution. I think we had better leave our principal speeches until the second reading of the bill. We heard this afternoon a most informative, and I for one think a most courageous, speech by the member for the Yukon. There is no doubt that from the information he gave to the committee and from the information which other hon. members have received he was speaking for a great majority of the people whom he represents. While I was listening to him I thought that he must have inherited his father's independence. His father was a federal government official on the Arrow lakes in the early days of this century and was well known for the strong stands he took on issues about which he felt keenly.
Like the hon. member for the Yukon, I have every respect for the minister and I am confident that he is concerned about the proper development of Canadian natural resources. He has evidenced interest in the subject in general and has shown concern about certain developments in connection with the Columbia river. We appreciate that interest and that concern. I think other hon. members will agree with me when I say that I think in this instance the minister is receiving poor advice from his officials, and is accepting that advice. I think a reconsideration of the whole matter would be fully justified.
I notice that the Minister of Fisheries has stayed in the chamber this afternoon. The Minister of Fisheries has the ability to appear to be reading a document in a most interested manner when in fact he is listening intently to what is going on. I have experienced that on former occasions. I am quite sure that the Minister of Fisheries is very interested in 50433-260
Yukon Quartz Mining Act this matter and could make a most interesting speech on the question of the mining laws of British Columbia.
The minister is a mining engineer and for some years was secretary to the minister of mines of the province of British Columbia. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned, we had great difficulty with the mining laws of British Columbia until the early days of this century. Then under the McBride administration the mining laws were redrafted and they remained almost unchanged until a Liberal government came into power in British Columbia. The minister will remember that after some years the Liberal government made several amendments to the basic mining laws of the province which were required because of changing conditions and circumstances. I well remember the minister of mines making a speech in the provincial riding of Nelson-Creston where there is considerable mining activity. This was a meeting of mining men and I remember him saying that in his opinion British Columbia had the finest mining laws in Canada. I wonder if the Minister of Fisheries will disagree with that statement today. I should like to hear the Minister of Fisheries express an opinion on British Columbia mining laws.
The hon. member for the Yukon has pointed out that the basic law in the Yukon is based to some extent upon the experience in connection with the mining legislation in British Columbia because of the similarity between mining conditions and the terrain in British Columbia and the Yukon. When we have the finest mining legislation in Canada in British Columbia, according to the opinion expressed by a cabinet minister of a Liberal government in British Columbia, I cannot for the life of me understand why this government wants to change the situation and impose a different type of legislation in the Yukon.
I know that many hon. members on this side of the house appreciate that the hon. member for the Yukon is taking objection to this legislation because of the satisfaction they have had with the present law, which to a large extent is based upon the mining laws of British Columbia which a member of a Liberal government in British Columbia stated were the finest mining laws in Canada. I can understand the hon. member objecting to any change being made, but I think his main argument on this occasion is that he is speaking for the people of the Yukon and that the government in introducing this legislation has overlooked completely or disregarded completely the wishes of the majority of the people in the Yukon.
The hon. member referred to the opposition of the Yukon territorial council, an elected

Yukon Quartz Mining Act body that surely expresses the opinion of those concerned with mining in the Yukon, being close to them. Then, as the hon. member said, there is strong opposition from the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that it was because this chamber of mines functions on behalf of British Columbia and the Yukon, because the conditions are very similar and they represent people who have similar problems and a similar attitude to basic mining law and to mining legislation. We have the branches of the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines at Vancouver, the chamber itself, the central body, the branch at Whitehorse and the branch at Dawson City also expressing opposition to this legislation. Here we have the parent body and the body at the Yukon and the local bodies which are in touch with the mining situation and the two major towns in the Yukon, Whitehorse and Dawson, expressing opposition. We have the chamber of commerce at Mayo also opposed, and the board of trade of Whitehorse; and then various meetings of rank and file miners have expressed their opposition to this legislation. There have been many other individuals also, including prospectors, mining engineers, geologists and individual mine operators.
That is a massive weight of evidence and a massive weight of opposition against this legislation. For the life of me, I cannot understand the minister proceeding with this bill in view of the apparent opposition of the great majority of the people in the Yukon Territory.
The minister referred to the Cole report as being the basis for this legislation. I have a copy of the Cole report here and have read it through once or twice. In mentioning that he based the legislation on the Cole report, the minister did not deal very fully with a report made in reply to the Cole report by Dr. William V. Smitheringale, entitled "An Analysis of the Report on Matters Concerned with Administration of Quartz and Placer Mining in the Yukon Territory". This qualified engineer-I judge with a great deal of support, according to the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon-expresses some severe criticism of Mr. Cole's proposals. As far as I can understand from listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon, Mr. Cole is a highly qualified man in certain fields but he visited the Yukon only for a short period. I think I am correct in saying that. He based his report on that brief visit, whereas this other gentleman bases his reply to this report on long knowledge of and experience in Yukon mining conditions.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, in view of the opposition of the people of the Yukon, and in view of the fact that this legislation will replace legislation that has proven so satisfactory throughout the years, that the minister would be well advised to let the bill lie on the table for another session so that all those interested will have an opportunity to go into the matter and make their representations to the government, and so that members of the opposition and people in the country generally who have come to realize that the government, in pressing this legislation, is doing so in a most undemocratic way in opposition to the expressed wishes of the great majority in the territory that the legislation is intended to cover, will be considered.

Mr. Chairman, I am certainly not going to take up very much time this afternoon, and I do not intend to repeat the arguments that have been so well put forward in this house today. It seems to me that it took a great deal of courage on the part of the hon. member for the Yukon in one way, and then when you look at it in another way, anyone who has the backing of all the people of the Yukon Territory must, of course, voice his opinion according to their wishes. I grant you that that has not been the case always on the part of members of the house. Therefore I should like to commend him for his stand and the action he has taken here this afternoon.
He has given us a full and informative address, laying before us those things which concern his people in the Yukon and presenting a realistic approach to the problems with documented evidence. We in this house must take full recognition of those things he has laid before us in his well rounded discussion of these problems. It is apparent that the people of the Yukon were not consulted, according to the evidence that has been presented. Of course, I am not too surprised, because I can think of several cases during this session already where the people concerned have been left out in the cold in regard to being consulted until some unwarranted action has been taken by this government. Now they are making retractions. That was done in the case of Bill No. 3, and also the act relating to the consolidation of the Railway Act. Mr. Chairman, I am reluctant to take part in this debate, chiefly because the Minister of Fisheries indicated that my friend, the hon. member for Yukon, should beware of Greeks bearing gifts. Certainly I hope that anything I shall say will in no way embarrass him, in his very honest effort to convey to the minister the true feelings of his constituents. Yes, it may be unusual that someone from the banks of the Humber might be speaking about something that takes place on the banks of the Liard or of some other river. I listened with considerable interest to the minister both last night and today, and I made fairly full notes on what the minister had to say. As I glanced through them, I have wondered if there has been any connection between the reasons which he has given for the necessity of bringing in this new act and the actual reasons. I might take a look at a few of them.
First of all, he said that the Yukon had some unusual characteristics. Second, he said that mining legislation usually came within the jurisdiction of the province and that it was unusual that federal legislation was required. Third, he said that the territorial council handled certain matters of administration in the territory but were not seized of the right to legislate in connection with mining claims. He said that the natural resources were a federal job. He traced the history of the legislation dealing with mining. He indicated that we had had this act almost 50433-260J
Yukon Quartz Mining Act without change since 1924. I understand there have been seven subamendments since that time. He said that conditions have changed. He is not sure whether this act is fair to the mining prospectors at the present time. He said revision is required. All of these statements are about as wide as you could possibly make them but none of them discloses an inherent reason for changing this legislation. The minister referred to Colonel Cole's report. One of the most striking paragraphs in this report, in my opinion, is to be found at page 3, at about the sixth or seventh line:
There is in the Yukon an inherent determination that an act should prevail. While I do not share that feeling with the mining people of the Yukon I am of the opinion that a compromise, mutually satisfactory to the government of Canada and the people of the Yukon Territory can be devised.
Just what state have we reached in connection with the administration of the affairs of the people of this country when we have to reach a compromise between the wishes of the people and those of the government? I was always led to believe that the government reflected the wishes of the people. Here we have a situation where we are apparently now going to be asked to arbitrate between the wishes of the people of the Yukon and the wishes of the administration, as reflected in this new legislation proposed by the minister.
It is indicated that certain changes must be made. I have heard about two-post staking and I have heard about four-post staking. The conclusion that I have come to is that the only experience displayed by those who advocate four-post staking must have been obtained in a four-poster in a Whitehorse hotel. The indication that two-post staking is not adequate for this job is the contention that it is holding up development by new scientific methods. Yet the minister has said that there is no intention to give out concessions of any kind under this act. Surely that is where scientific development and the new methods of using scintillometers and other equipment of that kind would be reflected. He has said that there is no intention to make any concession to people who might be using those types of methods.
As a matter of fact, everyone should take the opportunity of going to the Yukon. You will find that it is not necessary to have large development companies take over this type of exploration. All this type of the newest and latest equipment can be handled by the new type of prospector. On the Liard in northern British Columbia, in the corner of the Yukon, I have seen six and seven private aircraft sitting there waiting to go on with a prospecting program, each one handled on the basis of an individual partnership of

Yukon Quartz Mining Act prospector and pilot, and each one having at its disposal some of the latest type of prospecting equipment. Apparently there can be no reason for revision on that score.
Then we find that it is indicated that two-post claims result in the fractional or marginal type of mining claims. I might refer the minister to the mining act of the province of Ontario which is contained in chapter 236 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1950. There he can see that, even with established townships and places where bearings can be taken for surveying, that act as well indicates that even with the four-post type of mining claims in Ontario, fractional claims may exist even there.

Then he talked about the question of the work involved in this type of mining claim. When we talk about two-posters and four-posters, I think there is an inclination to believe that we are just doubling the amount of work and that that is not too much. Leaving aside the question of the character of the country which has been described by every hon. member who has spoken so far, the fact is that there is probably four times as much actual physical work and expense involved; and in a territory of the type of that in which these mining prospectors are working, it becomes a heavy time-consuming and expensive proposition.
Then it has been indicated that this question of doing work on the claims is one which is difficult to check under present circumstances and that with the use of regulations we are going to be able to handle the matter a great deal better. Let us be frank about it. No matter whether it is an act or a regulation, there are people who will undoubtedly attempt to get by, if they can, without doing the work. British Columbia has spot checking in connection with development work on claims. I would strongly suggest to the minister that he might take some of his help, who have been so good at drafting this type of legislation, and send them out for a few months to handle the spot checking chore in the Yukon. If he did that, I am quite sure that they would not be quite so anxious to get us into regulations in this connection.
I am wondering whether, in fact, this legislation is not the thin edge of the wedge. When there is an undertaking that no concessions will be granted, I am wondering whether that does not mean there will be no concessions granted in the immediate
[Mr. Hamilton (York West).)
future but that, with regulations being provided under the new legislation, such concessions may be granted in the future without reference back to the house. I can understand there may be companies which are quite definitely interested in this type of legislation. I listened to the hon. member for the Yukon read the list of those who support his viewpoint. He covered pretty well most of the substantial and practical mining development and exploration companies. I wonder whether this type of legislation is not much more pleasant to those who make their living by taking the sucker's dollar, whether they be from Bay street or anywhere else, by simply selling something off a map. Of course this legislation would assist them to a great extent. They could sit in their offices and sell the best of claims simply from a piece of parchment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL EXISTING LEGISLATION AND SUBSTITUTE NEW ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I find myself
becoming increasingly interested in the subject matter of the resolution before the house this afternoon, and increasingly inclined to agree with the proposition advanced that this is not a piece of legislation which should be rushed through the house at this time. I do not know what percentage of the members of the house have the necessary qualifications to deal with this kind of legislation, qualifications such as the hon. member for Kootenay West suggested the Minister of Fisheries had, but certainly when this matter affects so vitally the people of the Yukon, who can only speak in this parliament through the voice of one representative, and is a matter which also involves complicated considerations in respect of mining, I feel the house should hesitate to rush into a decision so obviously contrary to the wishes of most of the people of the Yukon Territory.
Reference has already been made to the connection between mining law and conditions in the Yukon Territory and those of British Columbia, and I suppose that may tend to have the effect of making British Columbia members rather prone to take the position that extension of the basic mining law of British Columbia into the Yukon Territory is the logical and most desirable method of approaching the question. On the other hand, I for one am not inclined to say that is necessarily and irrevocably the case. Nevertheless, from such limited experience as I have had of the operation of the mining laws of British Columbia, I do feel that the statement made by the hon. member for Kootenay West, which he claimed had been vouched for on the authority of a Liberal minister of mines of British Columbia, is one with which we can agree to a great extent.

Certainly 1 suggest no one can claim that mining development in the province of British Columbia has been materially held back, nor have I been able to see any great reluctance on the part of some of the mining interests, to which the hon. member for Yancouver-Quadra referred, to come into our province because of the particular type of mining law we have there. I had very limited experience in doing a little two-post staking several years ago, and while I do not claim that that in any sense makes me an authority or puts me in the class of having been a professional prospector, nevertheless I do know enough about the matter to realize that the argument being advanced that in mountainous and rocky terrain the two-post staking system has advantages has a good deal of basis in fact.
I know that particularly if one is trying to travel over that type of terrain on snow-shoes and through underbrush it is much easier to do a proper job on one line than on a multitude of lines. I am quite interested in the fact that someone like Dr. Smithering-ale should have taken the trouble to make an analysis of the report submitted to the government by Dr. George E. Cole, which analysis indicates that the conclusions reached by Dr. Cole with respect to the Yukon situation do not necessarily represent the only valid conclusions that can be drawn. In his report Dr. Smitheringale discusses the relative merits of two-post and four-post staking, and points out that the conditions imposed upon an individual by mountainous terrain are really different from those prevailing in the flatter country characteristic of most of Canada east of the Rocky mountains. In that regard he says:
The four-posters readily admit there is less work involved with two posts, but overcome such an admission by stating a two-post claim is not properly staked, is poorly defined . . .
Later in his report Dr. Smitheringale comes out quite bluntly and says:
Moreover, allow me to flatly contradict anyone who says a claim, staked by two posts, is not as rigidly defined as one staked by four. Colonel Cole, as well as all other responsible people, government or private, knows beyond argument that the boundaries of any claim or any plot of ground, no matter how staked, are not fully defined until such time as an accurate land survey has been made . . . and registered . . .
I lived in one of the mining areas of British Columbia during the time of a staking boom, and certainly my limited observation would indicate that what Dr. Smitheringale says is in point of fact borne out. I happen to know that Dr. Smitheringale is no newcomer to the mining game. It was in 1933 that I first met him. At that time he was the manager of a mine which was under
Yukon Quartz Mining Act development and was one of the people chosen by the British Columbia mining department to deliver lectures to prospectors on subjects which are of interest to them, under a plan carried on by the British Columbia department of mines. With a long experience in an area such as British Columbia, back of an experience in the Yukon Territory, I would suggest that Dr. Smitherin-gale's opinion in this connection may very well be as valid as the one that has been expressed by the engineer whose recommendation the government apparently is prepared to take.
I have quoted briefly from Dr. Smitherin-gale's remarks and tried to suggest to the house he is a man with sufficient qualifications to express an informed opinion, in order to further advance the argument that we in this house are getting into something of a very complex nature. It is a problem that could vitally affect the future of mining in the Yukon Territory, and one about which we should not be asked to hurriedly come to a decision in view of the objections which have already been raised to the proposed legislation. We all hope that this session is coming towards its close, and therefore the detailed work of committees should not be such as to prolong the sittings of committees at this time. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman that this is the type of bill that needs a detailed and thorough examination by a committee. It is the type of bill, as has been suggested, upon which all those concerned should have an opportunity of making representations and presenting their detailed briefs.
Under the present circumstances it would be most difficult for a committee of the house to give this bill the kind of consideration that it should have, and to bring in a report to the committee of the whole so that the measure could receive adequate consideration or amendment at this session For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I felt I should like to complement the remarks which were previously made by my colleague the hon member for Kootenay West. I feel that we who come from British Columbia have a very valid reason for believing we have good mining laws, mining laws which have been developed out of a long experience in the mining industry. These mining laws result from the fact that British Columbia, once it. passed the fur trading era, owes its very existence as a province to mining activities.
I know that in some respects we have always regarded the Yukon Territory as the child of British Columbia, especially so far as mining is concerned. I have heard old-timers in the Cariboo mining country tell:

Yukon Quartz Mining Act what happened when word of the discovery of gold in the Yukon reached that area. The placer miners dropped their tools and started the trek to the north. I suppose from that beginning mining in the Yukon and in British Columbia have had a closg association. It is not only the result of easily established lines of communication, but in large part a matter of the inherited tradition which was carried from British Columbia into the mining development of the country to the north of us.
So, Mr. Chairman, I feel it is not only fair but proper that, with that background, those of us who come from British Columbia should view with a rather jaundiced eye any proposal which would make the mining law of the Yukon Territory a basically different arrangement from that which we have in British Columbia.
